entries.title: Google Gemini Manual
entries.snippet: Accessible keyboard-first Google Gemini manual for blind and low-vision learners.
entries.text: google gemini manual google gemini manual accessible keyboard-first google gemini manual for blind and low-vision learners. google gemini manual - accessible learning center accessible google gemini course google gemini manual practical, responsible ai skills for work, learning, and independent problem-solving. basics prompting verification privacy screen readers lessons what generative ai does generative ai predicts and creates text or other content from patterns in training data and the information supplied in a conversation. it can help brainstorm, organize, explain, summarize, and draft. it does not understand a situation the way a person does, and it can produce confident but incorrect or invented information. use ai as an assistant, not as the final decision-maker. a person remains responsible for checking accuracy, appropriateness, accessibility, and compliance with workplace rules. a reliable prompt pattern task: state exactly what you want. context: explain the audience and purpose using nonprivate information. constraints: give length, tone, reading level, deadline, or other limits. format: request headings, bullets, a numbered procedure, or a simple table. checks: ask the tool to identify uncertainty and provide sources when appropriate. continue the conversation with specific follow-ups. for example: “shorten this to 150 words,” “explain the second step,” or “which statements need verification?” verify before using the result open original sources instead of trusting an ai summary or citation. confirm names, dates, quotations, calculations, contact details, laws, policies, and software instructions. prefer current primary sources from the organization responsible for the information. compare important claims with a second reliable source. test instructions safely before giving them to another person. rewrite the final result in your own voice and keep a record of corrections. privacy and workplace rules do not enter client records, medical or disability details, passwords, financial account information, private addresses, confidential workplace material, copyrighted documents you are not permitted to share, or information that identifies another person. use fictional or public information in these lessons. follow the employer’s approved-tool, retention, disclosure, and human-review requirements. a personal free account is not automatically approved for organizational data. never allow ai to make an employment, benefit, medical, legal, financial, safety, or accommodation decision for a person. accessible output ask for descriptive headings, short paragraphs, meaningful link text, numbered steps, and simple tables. ask for image descriptions when an image matters, but verify the description with a trusted person when accuracy is important. avoid layouts that communicate meaning only through color, position, or visual formatting. jaws, narrator, and nvda ai interfaces change often. use tab and shift+tab to move among controls, enter or space to activate a control, and the screen reader’s heading, landmark, link, button, edit-field, and browse-mode commands to review the page. use browser find to locate words such as “sources,” “copy,” or part of your prompt. jaws: h moves by heading, b by button, e by edit field, insert+f7 opens links, and insert+f5 opens form fields. nvda: h moves by heading, b by button, e by edit field, nvda+f7 opens the elements list, and nvda+space switches browse and focus modes. narrator: use caps lock or insert with arrow keys for scan mode navigation; press caps lock+space to toggle scan mode when needed. after sending a prompt, allow time for the response to finish. move by heading or paragraph and confirm whether focus changed. product-specific keyboard behavior may change after updates. free-course rule these lessons can be completed with an available free ai service or by studying the examples without creating an account. do not start a paid trial, enter payment information, or purchase a subscription for this course. official references official gemini apps help google: verify responses from gemini apps google gemini lessons lesson 1: open gemini and navigate the chat interface lesson 2: write prompts with purpose, context, and format lesson 3: refine a response through follow-up prompts lesson 4: create clear workplace checklists and plans lesson 5: summarize public web information and verify it lesson 6: draft content for google docs and gmail lesson 7: plan calendar tasks and spreadsheet information lesson 8: review sources, bias, and missing information lesson 9: use gemini with jaws, narrator, or nvda lesson 10: final google gemini workplace project start gemini lesson 1 all gemini lessons my entries.title: Screen Readers Lesson 1
entries.snippet: Accessible screen-reader Lesson 1: Choose, Start, and Stop a Screen Reader, with JAWS, Narrator, and NVDA options.
entries.text: screen readers lesson 1 screen readers lesson 1 accessible screen-reader lesson 1: choose, start, and stop a screen reader, with jaws, narrator, and nvda options. screen readers lesson 1 - accessible learning center screen readers course screen readers lesson 1 choose, start, and stop a screen reader screen readers manual all screen readers lessons my progress choose your screen reader complete this lesson with jaws, windows narrator, or nvda . use one primary screen reader at a time. follow the column for your selection whenever commands differ. goal choose jaws, narrator, or nvda and start and stop it safely. shared practice steps choose one primary screen reader for this course. do not run multiple screen readers at the same time unless an instructor directs you. confirm that the computer’s speakers or headset are connected and the volume is safe. start the selected screen reader using its method in the comparison table. open notepad and type one short sentence. confirm the screen reader announces the application, focus, and typed text. save the note and stop the screen reader using its documented method. jaws, narrator, and nvda comparison commands and differences for lesson 1 task jaws narrator nvda start search for jaws from start; a configured desktop shortcut may also be available. press windows+ctrl+enter. press ctrl+alt+n if the installation created that shortcut, or search for nvda from start. screen-reader modifier jaws key: insert; caps lock may be configured on laptops. narrator key: caps lock or insert by default. nvda key: insert or caps lock, based on keyboard layout. stop or exit press insert+f4 and confirm exit. press windows+ctrl+enter. press nvda+q and confirm exit. command note: jaws key, narrator key, and nvda key each mean that screen reader’s modifier key. commands can vary by keyboard layout, software version, application, and user settings. confirm differences in the official references linked from the manual. your assignment create a one-page choice report naming the selected screen reader, why it fits the practice computer, and how to start and stop it. use fictional, public, instructor-provided, or redacted information only. never submit passwords, license information, account codes, or private workplace data. save your work with a filename beginning screen-readers-lesson-1 . before submitting the selected screen reader is named. the commands match jaws, narrator, or nvda. shared windows commands are distinguished from screen-reader commands. the file contains no credentials or sensitive information. next lesson jaws lesson 1.html

press twice for browsable details where supported. command note: jaws key, narrator key, and nvda key each mean that screen reader’s modifier key. commands can vary by keyboard layout, software version, application, and user settings. confirm differences in the official references linked from the manual. your assignment revise an instructor-provided workplace memo and submit a command log plus the corrected copy. use fictional, public, instructor-provided, or redacted information only. never submit passwords, license information, account codes, or private workplace data. save your work with a filename beginning screen-readers-lesson-8 . before submitting the selected screen reader is named. the commands match jaws, narrator, or nvda. shared windows commands are distinguished from screen-reader commands. the file contains no credentials or sensitive information. previous lesson next lesson jaws lesson 8.html

entries.text: screen readers lesson 9 screen readers lesson 9 accessible screen-reader lesson 9: help, settings, updates, braille, and jaws ai, with jaws, narrator, and nvda options. screen readers lesson 9 - accessible learning center screen readers course screen readers lesson 9 help, settings, updates, braille, and jaws ai screen readers manual all screen readers lessons my progress choose your screen reader complete this lesson with jaws, windows narrator, or nvda . use one primary screen reader at a time. follow the column for your selection whenever commands differ. goal find trustworthy help, make reversible settings changes, and understand product-specific advanced features. shared practice steps open the selected screen reader’s settings or menu. locate speech, verbosity, keyboard-layout, and braille options without changing unrelated settings. change one instructor-approved reversible setting, test it, and restore the original. open the official help or current command reference. record the installed screen-reader version without including device serial numbers or license information. review the jaws-only ai note and do not assume the same feature exists in narrator or nvda. jaws, narrator, and nvda comparison commands and differences for lesson 9 task jaws narrator nvda settings or menu insert+j opens the jaws window; use options and help. insert+f2 opens the run jaws manager list. windows+ctrl+n opens narrator settings. nvda+n opens the nvda menu; preferences contains settings. command help insert+1 keyboard help and jaws help or fscompanion. narrator+1 input learning and microsoft’s narrator command guide. nvda+1 input help and the nvda user guide or commands quick reference. ai description fscompanion answers jaws questions, and picture smart ai describes images when available in the installed jaws version. follow current freedom scientific help and privacy rules. narrator does not provide the same jaws fscompanion or picture smart ai features. nvda core does not provide the same jaws features. do not install add-ons without authorization. command note: jaws key, narrator key, and nvda key each mean that screen reader’s modifier key. commands can vary by keyboard layout, software version, application, and user settings. confirm differences in the official references linked from the manual. your assignment create a comparison explaining official help, settings, updates, braille support, and which ai features are jaws-only. use fictional, public, instructor-provided, or redacted information only. never submit passwords, license information, account codes, or private workplace data. save your work with a filename beginning screen-readers-lesson-9 . before submitting the selected screen reader is named. the commands match jaws, narrator, or nvda. shared windows commands are distinguished from screen-reader commands. the file contains no credentials or sensitive information. previous lesson next lesson jaws lesson 9.html

entries.title: Screen Readers: JAWS, Narrator, and NVDA
entries.course: Screen Readers: JAWS, Narrator, and NVDA
entries.snippet: Accessible screen-reader manual comparing JAWS, Windows Narrator, and NVDA.
entries.text: screen readers manual screen readers: jaws, narrator, and nvda accessible screen-reader manual comparing jaws, windows narrator, and nvda. screen readers manual - accessible learning center foundational assistive technology manual screen readers: jaws, narrator, and nvda choose one screen reader and learn the same workplace skills with product-specific commands. all manuals ten screen readers lessons my progress choose the screen reader available to you three windows screen-reader choices screen reader best reason to choose it for this course important note jaws choose jaws when it is installed and licensed by you, your school, or your workplace. includes jaws-specific tools such as fscompanion and picture smart ai when available. windows narrator choose narrator when you need the screen reader built into windows 11. start or stop it with windows+ctrl+enter. its scan mode and views differ from jaws. nvda choose nvda when it is already installed or your organization approves the free, open-source windows screen reader. its browse mode and nvda modifier commands differ from jaws and narrator. use one primary screen reader at a time. running several simultaneously can produce overlapping speech and conflicting commands. an instructor may demonstrate a second product after the student can safely start, stop, and recover the primary choice. what stays the same windows and application commands such as tab, shift+tab, arrow keys, enter, spacebar, ctrl+c, ctrl+v, alt+tab, and windows+l usually stay the same. screen-reader commands differ when you request information, change reading modes, open element lists, adjust speech, or use product settings. equivalent concepts with different names screen-reader key: jaws key, narrator key, or nvda key. web-reading mode: jaws virtual cursor, narrator scan mode, or nvda browse mode. typing in forms: jaws forms mode, narrator with scan mode off, or nvda focus mode. command discovery: jaws keyboard help, narrator input learning, or nvda input help. ten-lesson learning path lesson 1: choose, start, and stop a screen reader — choose jaws, narrator, or nvda and start and stop it safely. lesson 2: keyboard help, speech control, and basic information — use keyboard help and control speech without losing focus. lesson 3: read by character, word, line, paragraph, and continuously — read and review text at several levels with the chosen screen reader. lesson 4: navigate windows, dialogs, and controls — move reliably through windows applications and identify focus. lesson 5: browse webpages by headings, links, lists, and landmarks — navigate structured webpages efficiently with the selected screen reader. lesson 6: complete forms and manage input modes — enter fictional information in web forms while controlling reading and typing modes. lesson 7: navigate tables, lists, and structured information — read relationships in tables and lists without losing row or column context. lesson 8: read, edit, and review workplace documents — use shared editing commands and screen-reader feedback in word or another document editor. lesson 9: help, settings, updates, braille, and jaws ai — find trustworthy help, make reversible settings changes, and understand product-specific advanced features. lesson 10: final screen-reader workplace project — complete a realistic windows, web, form, document, and troubleshooting workflow with the chosen screen reader. official references freedom scientific: navigating web pages with jaws freedom scientific: jaws reading commands microsoft: complete guide to narrator microsoft: narrator keyboard commands nv access: current nvda user guide nv access: current nvda commands quick reference progress preservation: this course replaces the former jaws-only presentation. existing jaws lesson submissions remain recognized in student progress. start screen readers lesson 1 return to manuals jaws manual.html

entries.title: LibreOffice Calc Manual
entries.snippet: Accessible keyboard-first LibreOffice Calc manual for blind and low-vision learners.
entries.text: libreoffice calc manual libreoffice calc manual accessible keyboard-first libreoffice calc manual for blind and low-vision learners. libreoffice calc manual - accessible learning center free accessible spreadsheets libreoffice calc manual no-cost office skills, accessible workflows, and microsoft-compatible file exchange. cost accessibility file formats screen readers compatibility lessons no-cost course rule this course must not require a purchase, subscription, paid trial, payment card, or new paid service. libreoffice is free and open source. google docs editors and microsoft 365 for the web have free account-based options, but internet access, account rules, storage limits, and available features can differ. use an employer-approved program and account for workplace information. a free personal account is not automatically approved for client or organizational data. accessibility comes before feature count before choosing a program, test the actual work tasks with the learner’s preferred screen reader, braille display, magnification, browser zoom, color settings, and keyboard. confirm that focus is announced, controls have useful names, editing feedback is understandable, and essential tasks do not require a mouse. use descriptive headings, real lists, clear table headers, meaningful links, alternative text, sufficient contrast, and logical reading order. do not communicate meaning only through color or visual position. run the program’s accessibility checker when available, but also perform a keyboard and screen-reader review. keep an original editable file before exporting pdf or converting formats. native and exchange formats libreoffice native formats odt for writer, ods for calc, and odp for impress preserve libreoffice editing features. microsoft exchange formats docx, xlsx, and pptx are often required by employers or instructors using microsoft 365. other formats csv carries plain spreadsheet data without formulas or formatting. pdf is useful for fixed-layout review but may be harder to edit and must be checked for accessibility. save the native version first. then save or download a separate exchange copy and review it in the receiving program whenever possible. jaws, narrator, and nvda interfaces vary by program and update. use tab and shift+tab for controls, arrow keys within menus and lists, enter or space to activate, alt or f10 for menus when supported, ctrl+s to save, ctrl+o to open, and ctrl+z to undo. listen for the current control name and state instead of memorizing screen position. jaws: use insert+t for the window title, insert+tab for focused-control information, and insert+1 for keyboard help. nvda: use nvda+t for the title, nvda+tab for focus, and nvda+1 for input help. narrator: use caps lock+t for the title and caps lock+1 for input learning. toggle scan mode only when the application or webpage requires it. browser-based editors may have their own screen-reader-support setting and keyboard shortcuts. read the current official help before changing screen-reader modes. compatibility review keep an untouched native copy. create a separate docx, xlsx, pptx, csv, or pdf copy. read every heading, cell range, slide title, link, table, image description, formula result, note, and page or slide count. check fonts, spacing, page breaks, charts, animations, formulas, comments, and accessibility metadata. correct the native file and export again rather than repeatedly converting the same exchange copy. never promise perfect compatibility without testing the actual document in the receiving software. privacy, accounts, and sharing use fictional or public information in these lessons. do not upload client records, medical or disability information, passwords, financial data, or confidential workplace material. for cloud tools, confirm the active account and sharing permission before entering content. for local tools, back up files to an approved location. entries.title: LibreOffice Impress Manual
entries.snippet: Accessible keyboard-first LibreOffice Impress manual for blind and low-vision learners.
entries.text: libreoffice impress manual libreoffice impress manual accessible keyboard-first libreoffice impress manual for blind and low-vision learners. libreoffice impress manual - accessible learning center free accessible presentations libreoffice impress manual no-cost office skills, accessible workflows, and microsoft-compatible file exchange. cost accessibility file formats screen readers compatibility lessons no-cost course rule this course must not require a purchase, subscription, paid trial, payment card, or new paid service. libreoffice is free and open source. google docs editors and microsoft 365 for the web have free account-based options, but internet access, account rules, storage limits, and available features can differ. use an employer-approved program and account for workplace information. a free personal account is not automatically approved for client or organizational data. accessibility comes before feature count before choosing a program, test the actual work tasks with the learner’s preferred screen reader, braille display, magnification, browser zoom, color settings, and keyboard. confirm that focus is announced, controls have useful names, editing feedback is understandable, and essential tasks do not require a mouse. use descriptive headings, real lists, clear table headers, meaningful links, alternative text, sufficient contrast, and logical reading order. do not communicate meaning only through color or visual position. run the program’s accessibility checker when available, but also perform a keyboard and screen-reader review. keep an original editable file before exporting pdf or converting formats. native and exchange formats libreoffice native formats odt for writer, ods for calc, and odp for impress preserve libreoffice editing features. microsoft exchange formats docx, xlsx, and pptx are often required by employers or instructors using microsoft 365. other formats csv carries plain spreadsheet data without formulas or formatting. pdf is useful for fixed-layout review but may be harder to edit and must be checked for accessibility. save the native version first. then save or download a separate exchange copy and review it in the receiving program whenever possible. jaws, narrator, and nvda interfaces vary by program and update. use tab and shift+tab for controls, arrow keys within menus and lists, enter or space to activate, alt or f10 for menus when supported, ctrl+s to save, ctrl+o to open, and ctrl+z to undo. listen for the current control name and state instead of memorizing screen position. jaws: use insert+t for the window title, insert+tab for focused-control information, and insert+1 for keyboard help. nvda: use nvda+t for the title, nvda+tab for focus, and nvda+1 for input help. narrator: use caps lock+t for the title and caps lock+1 for input learning. toggle scan mode only when the application or webpage requires it. browser-based editors may have their own screen-reader-support setting and keyboard shortcuts. read the current official help before changing screen-reader modes. compatibility review keep an untouched native copy. create a separate docx, xlsx, pptx, csv, or pdf copy. read every heading, cell range, slide title, link, table, image description, formula result, note, and page or slide count. check fonts, spacing, page breaks, charts, animations, formulas, comments, and accessibility metadata. correct the native file and export again rather than repeatedly converting the same exchange copy. never promise perfect compatibility without testing the actual document in the receiving software. privacy, accounts, and sharing use fictional or public information in these lessons. do not upload client records, medical or disability information, passwords, financial data, or confidential workplace material. for cloud tools, confirm the active account and sharing permission before entering content. for local tools, back up files to an approved location. entries.title: LibreOffice Writer Manual
entries.snippet: Accessible keyboard-first LibreOffice Writer manual for blind and low-vision learners.
entries.text: libreoffice writer manual libreoffice writer manual accessible keyboard-first libreoffice writer manual for blind and low-vision learners. libreoffice writer manual - accessible learning center free accessible word processing libreoffice writer manual no-cost office skills, accessible workflows, and microsoft-compatible file exchange. cost accessibility file formats screen readers compatibility lessons no-cost course rule this course must not require a purchase, subscription, paid trial, payment card, or new paid service. libreoffice is free and open source. google docs editors and microsoft 365 for the web have free account-based options, but internet access, account rules, storage limits, and available features can differ. use an employer-approved program and account for workplace information. a free personal account is not automatically approved for client or organizational data. accessibility comes before feature count before choosing a program, test the actual work tasks with the learner’s preferred screen reader, braille display, magnification, browser zoom, color settings, and keyboard. confirm that focus is announced, controls have useful names, editing feedback is understandable, and essential tasks do not require a mouse. use descriptive headings, real lists, clear table headers, meaningful links, alternative text, sufficient contrast, and logical reading order. do not communicate meaning only through color or visual position. run the program’s accessibility checker when available, but also perform a keyboard and screen-reader review. keep an original editable file before exporting pdf or converting formats. native and exchange formats libreoffice native formats odt for writer, ods for calc, and odp for impress preserve libreoffice editing features. microsoft exchange formats docx, xlsx, and pptx are often required by employers or instructors using microsoft 365. other formats csv carries plain spreadsheet data without formulas or formatting. pdf is useful for fixed-layout review but may be harder to edit and must be checked for accessibility. save the native version first. then save or download a separate exchange copy and review it in the receiving program whenever possible. jaws, narrator, and nvda interfaces vary by program and update. use tab and shift+tab for controls, arrow keys within menus and lists, enter or space to activate, alt or f10 for menus when supported, ctrl+s to save, ctrl+o to open, and ctrl+z to undo. listen for the current control name and state instead of memorizing screen position. jaws: use insert+t for the window title, insert+tab for focused-control information, and insert+1 for keyboard help. nvda: use nvda+t for the title, nvda+tab for focus, and nvda+1 for input help. narrator: use caps lock+t for the title and caps lock+1 for input learning. toggle scan mode only when the application or webpage requires it. browser-based editors may have their own screen-reader-support setting and keyboard shortcuts. read the current official help before changing screen-reader modes. compatibility review keep an untouched native copy. create a separate docx, xlsx, pptx, csv, or pdf copy. read every heading, cell range, slide title, link, table, image description, formula result, note, and page or slide count. check fonts, spacing, page breaks, charts, animations, formulas, comments, and accessibility metadata. correct the native file and export again rather than repeatedly converting the same exchange copy. never promise perfect compatibility without testing the actual document in the receiving software. privacy, accounts, and sharing use fictional or public information in these lessons. do not upload client records, medical or disability information, passwords, financial data, or confidential workplace material. for cloud tools, confirm the active account and sharing permission before entering content. for local tools, back up files to an approved location. styles, and document navigation lesson 6: create lists and accessible tables lesson 7: add links, images, and alternative text lesson 8: run the accessibility check and export pdf/ua lesson 9: open accessible presentation. skills practiced plan a logical presentation structure. use layouts, titles, lists, links, and visuals accessibly. verify reading order and alternative text. present with keyboard commands and speaker notes. step-by-step instructions create a presentation for a fictional new-employee orientation. include a title slide and at least six additional slides. cover welcome, daily schedule, workplace expectations, technology resources, safety or emergency information, and contact information. use built-in layouts and give every slide a unique title. include at least one meaningful image with alt text. include either an accessible table or a chart with alt text, source values, and a text summary. include at least one meaningful hyperlink. check the reading order on every slide. use strong contrast and do not communicate by color alone. add concise speaker notes to every content slide. run check accessibility and resolve applicable errors and warnings. present entries.snippet: Accessible Microsoft PowerPoint Lesson 3: Text, Bullets, and Clear Slide Content.
entries.text: powerpoint lesson 3 powerpoint lesson 3 accessible microsoft powerpoint lesson 3: text, bullets, and clear slide content. powerpoint lesson 3 - accessible learning center microsoft powerpoint course powerpoint lesson 3 text, bullets, and clear slide content powerpoint manual all powerpoint lessons my progress goal create concise, structured slide text that works for screen-reader users and visual audiences. skills practiced enter text in placeholders. create bulleted and numbered lists. change bullet levels with tab and shift+tab. keep slide language concise and meaningful. step-by-step instructions create a new presentation with the title accessible customer service. add a slide titled greeting a customer. enter three bullets: introduce yourself, ask how you can help, and listen before responding. with focus in the second bullet, press tab to create a sub-bullet and type clarify the request. press shift+tab if you need to return it to the main level. add a slide titled resolving a request. create a numbered list with four steps: identify the problem, confirm the desired result, complete the action, and verify satisfaction. avoid long paragraphs. keep each bullet to one clear idea. use ctrl+b only when emphasis adds meaning; do not rely on bold alone to communicate status. review each text object by pressing tab through the slide, then f2 or enter to edit its text. save the presentation as powerpoint-lesson-3.pptx. keyboard help: press alt+q to search powerpoint commands when ribbon keytips differ. for jaws help, press insert+spacebar, then j, and search for the task. your assignment create a three-slide customer-service presentation containing a title slide, a bulleted process, and a numbered process. save the finished assignment as powerpoint-lesson-3.pptx . before submitting all three slides have unique titles. bullets and numbering are used appropriately. text is concise and understandable out of visual context. the file is saved as powerpoint-lesson-3.pptx. previous lesson next lesson powerpoint lesson 3.html

entries.snippet: Accessible Microsoft PowerPoint Lesson 4: Images, Alternative Text, and Decorative Objects.
entries.text: powerpoint lesson 4 powerpoint lesson 4 accessible microsoft powerpoint lesson 4: images, alternative text, and decorative objects. powerpoint lesson 4 - accessible learning center microsoft powerpoint course powerpoint lesson 4 images, alternative text, and decorative objects powerpoint manual all powerpoint lessons my progress goal insert an image and make its meaning available to people who cannot see it. skills practiced insert a picture with keyboard-accessible commands. select slide objects with tab. add concise alternative text. mark purely decorative objects appropriately. step-by-step instructions open powerpoint-lesson-3.pptx and add a slide titled accessible communication. press alt+q, type insert pictures, and choose the appropriate command. insert a locally available, nonprivate image related to communication or technology. press tab until jaws announces the picture object. press shift+f10 to open the context menu. choose view alt text or edit alt text. write concise alt text explaining the image's purpose in the slide. do not begin with image of unless that wording adds meaning. if you add a purely decorative shape, mark it as decorative in the alt text pane when that option is available. add a visible caption only if the audience needs additional context. press tab through every object and confirm that jaws identifies it. run alt+q, check accessibility and review image-related warnings. save the presentation as powerpoint-lesson-4.pptx. keyboard help: press alt+q to search powerpoint commands when ribbon keytips differ. for jaws help, press insert+spacebar, then j, and search for the task. your assignment add one meaningful image with useful alternative text to the customer-service presentation and review it with accessibility checker. save the finished assignment as powerpoint-lesson-4.pptx . before submitting the image supports the slide's message. the image has concise, meaningful alt text. decorative objects are marked decorative when appropriate. accessibility checker was reviewed. the file is saved as powerpoint-lesson-4.pptx. previous lesson next lesson powerpoint lesson 4.html

entries.title: PowerPoint Lesson 5
entries.snippet: Accessible Microsoft PowerPoint Lesson 5: Reading Order and Keyboard Navigation.
entries.text: powerpoint lesson 5 powerpoint lesson 5 accessible microsoft powerpoint lesson 5: reading order and keyboard navigation. powerpoint lesson 5 - accessible learning center microsoft powerpoint course powerpoint lesson 5 reading order and keyboard navigation powerpoint manual all powerpoint lessons my progress goal arrange slide objects so a screen reader encounters them in a logical order. skills practiced understand object reading order. use the reading order pane. test slides with tab and shift+tab. keep slide titles first in the logical sequence. step-by-step instructions open powerpoint-lesson-4.pptx. choose a slide containing a title, text, and image. press alt+q, type reading order, and open the reading order pane or use the accessibility checker recommendation. review the listed objects. the title should be read before the main content, and supporting objects should follow logically. use the pane's move up and move down controls to correct the sequence if needed. mark decorative objects decorative rather than leaving them unnamed. close the pane and return to the slide. press tab repeatedly to test the object sequence. use shift+tab to move backward. repeat the test on every slide. run check accessibility and resolve reading-order warnings that apply. save the presentation as powerpoint-lesson-5.pptx. keyboard help: press alt+q to search powerpoint commands when ribbon keytips differ. for jaws help, press insert+spacebar, then j, and search for the task. your assignment review and correct the reading order of every slide in the customer-service presentation. save the finished assignment as powerpoint-lesson-5.pptx . before submitting every slide has a title. titles occur before related slide content in reading order. tab navigation follows a logical sequence. decorative items do not interrupt the meaningful content. the file is saved as powerpoint-lesson-5.pptx. previous lesson next lesson powerpoint lesson 5.html

entries.title: PowerPoint Lesson 6
entries.snippet: Accessible Microsoft PowerPoint Lesson 6: Accessible Tables and Charts.
entries.text: powerpoint lesson 6 powerpoint lesson 6 accessible microsoft powerpoint lesson 6: accessible tables and charts. powerpoint lesson 6 - accessible learning center microsoft powerpoint course powerpoint lesson 6 accessible tables and charts powerpoint manual all powerpoint lessons my progress goal present structured data with clear headers, accessible descriptions, and a text summary. skills practiced insert a simple table. use a header row. create a chart from clear source data. add alt text and a text equivalent. step-by-step instructions create a presentation titled monthly training report. add a slide titled training completion table. use alt+q to find insert table. create a table with three columns and five rows. enter the headers month, enrolled, and completed in the first row. enter fictional data for january through april. confirm that the first row is designated as a header row through table design options. add a slide titled completion trend. create a simple chart from the same data using insert chart and its data worksheet. add alt text describing the chart's purpose and main trend. keep the table slide so exact values remain available. add a short text statement on the chart slide summarizing the trend without relying on color. run check accessibility and review the table and chart. save the presentation as powerpoint-lesson-6.pptx. keyboard help: press alt+q to search powerpoint commands when ribbon keytips differ. for jaws help, press insert+spacebar, then j, and search for the task. your assignment create a training report containing an accessible table, a chart with alt text, and a plain-text trend summary. save the finished assignment as powerpoint-lesson-6.pptx . before submitting the table has descriptive column headers. the chart has meaningful alt text. exact values remain available in the table. the trend is explained in text. the file is saved as powerpoint-lesson-6.pptx. previous lesson next lesson powerpoint lesson 6.html

entries.snippet: Accessible Microsoft PowerPoint Lesson 8: Color, Contrast, Fonts, and Accessible Design.
entries.text: powerpoint lesson 8 powerpoint lesson 8 accessible microsoft powerpoint lesson 8: color, contrast, fonts, and accessible design. powerpoint lesson 8 - accessible learning center microsoft powerpoint course powerpoint lesson 8 color, contrast, fonts, and accessible design powerpoint manual all powerpoint lessons my progress goal apply a professional design that remains readable with low vision and does not communicate by color alone. skills practiced use a consistent built-in theme. check text and background contrast. use readable font sizes. add text labels for color-coded information. step-by-step instructions open powerpoint-lesson-7.pptx. use alt+q to search for themes and choose a simple built-in theme. keep body text large enough to read from a distance. use approximately 18 points or larger for body text and larger sizes for titles when the layout allows. keep strong contrast between text and its background. do not place text over a busy image unless a solid background makes it readable. if a status is shown in red, yellow, or green, also write words such as needs action, in progress, or complete. avoid rapidly flashing content and excessive animations. keep the same typeface and heading treatment across slides. review each slide at increased zoom and with jaws object navigation. run check accessibility and fix contrast or color-use warnings when available. save the presentation as powerpoint-lesson-8.pptx. keyboard help: press alt+q to search powerpoint commands when ribbon keytips differ. for jaws help, press insert+spacebar, then j, and search for the task. your assignment apply a consistent, high-contrast design to the employee-resources presentation and ensure no meaning depends on color alone. save the finished assignment as powerpoint-lesson-8.pptx . before submitting text and backgrounds have strong contrast. body text is readable and not crowded. color-coded information also includes text labels. the design is consistent across slides. the file is saved as powerpoint-lesson-8.pptx. previous lesson next lesson powerpoint lesson 8.html

add useful speaker notes to every content slide and practice delivering the presentation entirely with the keyboard. save the finished assignment as powerpoint-lesson-9.pptx . before submitting every entries.title: Microsoft PowerPoint Accessible Manual
entries.snippet: Accessible Microsoft PowerPoint manual for Microsoft 365 desktop on Windows with JAWS and keyboard-first instruction.
entries.text: microsoft powerpoint manual microsoft powerpoint accessible manual accessible microsoft powerpoint manual for microsoft 365 desktop on windows with jaws and keyboard-first instruction. microsoft powerpoint manual - accessible learning center keyboard-first microsoft 365 training microsoft powerpoint accessible manual create, review, and present accessible slide decks with jaws and the keyboard. keyboard quick reference accessible slide practices course lessons about this manual this manual targets powerpoint in microsoft 365 desktop on windows. powerpoint contains several work areas, including the thumbnails pane, slide editing area, notes pane, and ribbon. press f6 to move among these areas and tab or shift+tab to move among objects on a slide. use built-in slide layouts whenever possible. layout placeholders provide structure that is easier to navigate and maintain than manually positioned text boxes. give every slide a unique, descriptive title. keyboard quick reference common powerpoint commands used in this course task command move among powerpoint panes f6 or shift+f6 move among slide objects tab or shift+tab create a new slide ctrl+m duplicate a selected slide or object ctrl+d move to next or previous slide in thumbnails down arrow or up arrow edit text in a selected placeholder enter or f2 exit text editing and select the object escape insert or edit a hyperlink ctrl+k save ctrl+s save as f12 start slide show from beginning f5 start slide show from current slide shift+f5 advance during slide show right arrow, spacebar, or page down move backward during slide show left arrow, backspace, or page up end slide show escape temporarily show a black screen b search office commands alt+q search jaws commands insert+spacebar, then j accessible slide practices use built-in slide layouts and give every slide a unique title. keep text concise and use real bulleted or numbered lists. maintain strong contrast and do not use color as the only way to communicate meaning. add concise alternative text to meaningful pictures, charts, shapes, and other visual objects. mark objects decorative only when they add no information. use the reading order pane to arrange objects logically, with the title before related content. use simple tables with a designated header row. avoid merged or split cells. for charts, retain source values and add a plain-text summary of the important result. use meaningful link text that identifies the destination. add speaker-note prompts to describe visuals aloud during a presentation. avoid flashing content and unnecessary animation. run check accessibility and test the entire deck with the keyboard. reading order screen readers follow the slide's object order, which may differ from the visual arrangement. open the reading order pane through alt+q or an accessibility checker recommendation, then move objects into a logical sequence. test that sequence by pressing tab through the slide. images, tables, and charts alt text should explain why a visual matters in the presentation. it should be concise, specific, and based on the presentation context. a chart needs alt text plus access to exact source values and a short text summary. a table needs clear headers and a simple structure. presenting accessibly start the slide show with f5, move with the arrow keys, and press escape to finish. speak important information shown in images, charts, and demonstrations. do not ask the audience to identify information only by color, position, or appearance. ten-lesson course sequence lesson 1: powerpoint basics: slides, placeholders, and saving — create a basic presentation, move among slide placeholders with the keyboard, and save the file. lesson 2: slide layouts, titles, and organizing a presentation — use built-in slide layouts and meaningful titles to create a clear presentation structure. lesson 3: text, bullets, and clear slide content — create concise, structured slide text that works for screen-reader users and visual audiences. lesson 4: images, alternative text, and decorative objects — insert an image and make its meaning available to people who cannot see it. lesson 5: reading order and keyboard navigation — arrange slide objects so a screen reader encounters them in a logical order. lesson 6: accessible tables and charts — present structured data with clear headers, accessible descriptions, and a text summary. lesson 7: meaningful links and contact information — add links that clearly identify their destination and work with keyboard navigation. lesson 8: color, contrast, fonts, and accessible design — apply a professional design that remains readable with low vision and does not communicate by color alone. lesson 9: speaker notes and presenting with the keyboard — prepare concise speaker notes and deliver a presentation using keyboard commands. lesson 10: final accessible workplace presentation — independently create, check, and practice a professional accessible presentation. begin powerpoint lesson 1 official references and further learning microsoft: create accessible office documents microsoft: making documents accessible microsoft: add alternative text to objects microsoft: accessibility checker freedom scientific: jaws documentation view powerpoint lessons view my progress return to manuals powerpoint manual.html

entries.title: Google Sheets Manual
entries.snippet: Accessible keyboard-first Google Sheets manual for blind and low-vision learners.
entries.text: google sheets manual google sheets manual accessible keyboard-first google sheets manual for blind and low-vision learners. google sheets manual - accessible learning center free browser-based spreadsheets google sheets manual no-cost office skills, accessible workflows, and microsoft-compatible file exchange. cost accessibility file formats screen readers compatibility lessons no-cost course rule this course must not require a purchase, subscription, paid trial, payment card, or new paid service. libreoffice is free and open source. google docs editors and microsoft 365 for the web have free account-based options, but internet access, account rules, storage limits, and available features can differ. use an employer-approved program and account for workplace information. a free personal account is not automatically approved for client or organizational data. accessibility comes before feature count before choosing a program, test the actual work tasks with the learner’s preferred screen reader, braille display, magnification, browser zoom, color settings, and keyboard. confirm that focus is announced, controls have useful names, editing feedback is understandable, and essential tasks do not require a mouse. use descriptive headings, real lists, clear table headers, meaningful links, alternative text, sufficient contrast, and logical reading order. do not communicate meaning only through color or visual position. run the program’s accessibility checker when available, but also perform a keyboard and screen-reader review. keep an original editable file before exporting pdf or converting formats. native and exchange formats libreoffice native formats odt for writer, ods for calc, and odp for impress preserve libreoffice editing features. microsoft exchange formats docx, xlsx, and pptx are often required by employers or instructors using microsoft 365. other formats csv carries plain spreadsheet data without formulas or formatting. pdf is useful for fixed-layout review but may be harder to edit and must be checked for accessibility. save the native version first. then save or download a separate exchange copy and review it in the receiving program whenever possible. jaws, narrator, and nvda interfaces vary by program and update. use tab and shift+tab for controls, arrow keys within menus and lists, enter or space to activate, alt or f10 for menus when supported, ctrl+s to save, ctrl+o to open, and ctrl+z to undo. listen for the current control name and state instead of memorizing screen position. jaws: use insert+t for the window title, insert+tab for focused-control information, and insert+1 for keyboard help. nvda: use nvda+t for the title, nvda+tab for focus, and nvda+1 for input help. narrator: use caps lock+t for the title and caps lock+1 for input learning. toggle scan mode only when the application or webpage requires it. browser-based editors may have their own screen-reader-support setting and keyboard shortcuts. read the current official help before changing screen-reader modes. compatibility review keep an untouched native copy. create a separate docx, xlsx, pptx, csv, or pdf copy. read every heading, cell range, slide title, link, table, image description, formula result, note, and page or slide count. check fonts, spacing, page breaks, charts, animations, formulas, comments, and accessibility metadata. correct the native file and export again rather than repeatedly converting the same exchange copy. never promise perfect compatibility without testing the actual document in the receiving software. privacy, accounts, and sharing use fictional or public information in these lessons. do not upload client records, medical or disability information, passwords, financial data, or confidential workplace material. for cloud tools, confirm the active account and sharing permission before entering content. for local tools, back up files to an approved location. lesson 2: navigate cells, ranges, sheets, and menus lesson 3: enter, edit, fill, find, and format data lesson 4: create formulas and basic functions lesson 5: use accessible headers, names, and number formats lesson 6: sort, filter, and protect a data range lesson 7: use data validation and conditional results lesson 8: create a chart with an equivalent text summary lesson 9: share safely and export xlsx, csv, or pdf lesson 10: final accessible sheets workplace tracker start sheets lesson 1 all sheets lessons my progress sheets manual.html

lessons no-cost course rule this course must not require a purchase, subscription, paid trial, payment card, or new paid service. libreoffice is free and open source. google docs editors and microsoft 365 for the web have free account-based options, but internet access, account rules, storage limits, and available features can differ. use an employer-approved program and account for workplace information. a free personal account is not automatically approved for client or organizational data. accessibility comes before feature count before choosing a program, test the actual work tasks with the learner’s preferred screen reader, braille display, magnification, browser zoom, color settings, and keyboard. confirm that focus is announced, controls have useful names, editing feedback is understandable, and essential tasks do not require a mouse. use descriptive headings, real lists, clear table headers, meaningful links, alternative text, sufficient contrast, and logical reading order. do not communicate meaning only through color or visual position. run the program’s accessibility checker when available, but also perform a keyboard and screen-reader review. keep an original editable file before exporting pdf or converting formats. native and exchange formats libreoffice native formats odt for writer, ods for calc, and odp for impress preserve libreoffice editing features. microsoft exchange formats docx, xlsx, and pptx are often required by employers or instructors using microsoft 365. other formats csv carries plain spreadsheet data without formulas or formatting. pdf is useful for fixed-layout review but may be harder to edit and must be checked for accessibility. save the native version first. then save or download a separate exchange copy and review it in the receiving program whenever possible. jaws, narrator, and nvda interfaces vary by program and update. use tab and shift+tab for controls, arrow keys within menus and lists, enter or space to activate, alt or f10 for menus when supported, ctrl+s to save, ctrl+o to open, and ctrl+z to undo. listen for the current control name and state instead of memorizing screen position. jaws: use insert+t for the window title, insert+tab for focused-control information, and insert+1 for keyboard help. nvda: use nvda+t for the title, nvda+tab for focus, and nvda+1 for input help. narrator: use caps lock+t for the title and caps lock+1 for input learning. toggle scan mode only when the application or webpage requires it. browser-based editors may have their own screen-reader-support setting and keyboard shortcuts. read the current official help before changing screen-reader modes. compatibility review keep an untouched native copy. create a separate docx, xlsx, pptx, csv, or pdf comments, and accessibility metadata. correct the native file and export again rather than repeatedly converting the same exchange copy. never promise perfect compatibility without testing the actual document in the receiving software. privacy, accounts, and sharing use fictional or public information in these lessons. do not upload client records, medical or disability information, passwords, financial data, or confidential workplace material. for cloud tools, confirm the active account and sharing permission before entering content. for local tools, back up files to an approved location. moving: ctrl+x. paste: ctrl+v. properties: alt+enter. delete to recycle bin: delete. confirm the selection first. protect files: never approve an overwrite, delete a large selection, or empty the recycle bin until names, locations, and backups are confirmed. selection, search, and location awareness arrow keys move the current item. shift+arrow extends a continuous selection, ctrl+spacebar can change one item’s selection state, and ctrl+a selects all. before copying, moving, or deleting, confirm what is selected and which folder is open. search within a specific folder for faster, safer results. review file name, extension, type, date, and location before opening downloaded content. built-in accessibility features press windows+i and search for accessibility. windows includes
